FOUNDATIONS · CHAPTER 02 02 02 A vs B Decision Map 29 common choices: what each solves, when A wins, when B wins, and a default. INSIDE 29 decisions in 6 groups A vs B cards with a stated default How to write the choice into an ADR HOW TO USE Read this first Name the problem first. Check the constraints: team size, scale, consistency need, budget. Pick the simpler option unless a constraint rules it out. Write the choice and its revisit trigger in an ADR. DEFAULTS Every card ends with a default. Override it with evidence from your constraints, not with taste. Architecture ARCHITECTURE Monolith vs Microservices Monolith Microservices One team, domain still unclear, early product, simple ops. Independent deploys and scaling, many teams, stable service boundaries. R U L E Start with a modular monolith; split only when a boundary hurts. ARCHITECTURE Orchestration vs Choreography Orchestration Choreography Many steps, need central visibility and compensation logic. Few steps, loose coupling, teams own their reactions to events. R U L E Past about 4 steps, choreography becomes hard to trace. ARCHITECTURE Event sourcing vs CRUD + audit table Event sourcing CRUD + audit Need full history, temporal queries, replay, rebuildable views. Current state is enough; team new to the model. R U L E CRUD is the default; event sourcing is a deliberate cost. ARCHITECTURE CQRS vs Single model CQRS Single model Read and write shapes or loads diverge sharply. Plain CRUD with similar reads and writes. R U L E Add CQRS for a proven read bottleneck, not up front. ARCHITECTURE Serverless vs Containers / K8s Serverless Containers / K8s Spiky or rare load, short tasks, small ops team. Steady load, long-running work, runtime control, cost at scale. R U L E Compare cost at your steady-state volume, not at idle. Data D ATA SQL vs NoSQL SQL NoSQL Relations, transactions, adhoc queries, evolving questions. Known access patterns, huge scale, flexible schema, key-based access. R U L E Default to SQL until a measured limit says otherwise. D ATA Read replicas vs Sharding Read replicas Sharding Read-heavy; one node still holds the writes and data. Writes or data volume exceed one node. R U L E Replicas, then caching, then sharding. Sharding is the last step. D ATA Leader–follower vs Multi-leader / leaderless Leader–follower Multi / leaderless Single write region, simple conflict-free model. Multi-region writes or write availability during partitions; conflicts handled. R U L E Multi-leader means designing conflict resolution. D ATA Optimistic vs Pessimistic locking Optimistic Pessimistic Low contention; retries are cheap. High contention on hot rows; retries are costly. R U L E Version column first; lock only where conflicts are frequent. D ATA DB full-text search vs Search engine DB full-text Search engine Modest data, simple queries, one less system to run. Relevance ranking, facets, fuzzy match, large corpora. R U L E Keep search in the DB until relevance or scale demands more. D ATA Batch vs Stream Batch Stream Hours of latency is fine; completeness and simplicity matter. Seconds-level latency; continuous, event-time results. R U L E Streaming adds state, ordering and replay concerns. Messaging MESSAGING Kafka vs RabbitMQ Kafka RabbitMQ Replayable log, high throughput, many independent consumers, ordering per key. Task queues, rich routing, per-message ack and retry, priorities. R U L E Log of facts: Kafka. Queue of jobs: RabbitMQ. MESSAGING Kafka vs SQS + SNS Kafka SQS + SNS Replay, stream processing, ordered partitions, high volume. Managed simplicity, modest volume, no cluster to operate. R U L E Operating Kafka is a team cost; weigh managed options. MESSAGING Sync call vs Async messaging Sync call Async messaging Caller needs the answer now to continue. Work can finish later; decouple, absorb spikes, isolate failures. R U L E Async trades latency certainty for resilience. MESSAGING Polling vs Push (WS / SSE) Polling Push Infrequent updates, simple clients, tolerate delay. Frequent real-time updates; many clients watching changes. R U L E SSE for one-way feeds; WebSocket for two-way. APIs A P I S REST vs gRPC REST gRPC Public APIs, browsers, HTTP caching, wide tooling. Internal low-latency calls, streaming, strict contracts. R U L E External: REST. Internal hot paths: consider gRPC. A P I S REST vs GraphQL REST GraphQL Resource-shaped data, cacheable, simple clients. Many client shapes, aggregation across services, over-fetching pain. R U L E GraphQL moves complexity to caching, auth and N+1. A P I S JWT vs Server session JWT Server session Stateless services, crossservice identity, short lifetimes. Easy revocation, central control, single app. R U L E Short-lived JWT plus refresh; plan for revocation. Consistency CONSISTENCY Strong vs Eventual consistency Strong Eventual Money, inventory, uniqueness, anything unsafe to be stale. Feeds, counters, analytics, anything tolerating lag. R U L E Choose per entity, not per system. CONSISTENCY 2PC vs Saga 2PC Saga Few participants, same trust domain, XA support, short transactions. Cross-service, longrunning, availability over isolation. R U L E Saga needs idempotency and compensating actions. CONSISTENCY Cache-aside vs Write-through Cache-aside Write-through Read-heavy; stale-until-TTL is acceptable. Reads must reflect recent writes; accept write latency. R U L E Write-behind buys write speed at risk of loss. CONSISTENCY Redis vs Memcached Redis Memcached Data structures, persistence, pub/sub, replication, clustering. Plain multi-threaded keyvalue cache and nothing more. R U L E Redis covers more; Memcached is simpler when sufficient. Scale & Ops SCALE & OPS Vertical vs Horizontal scaling Vertical Horizontal Quick win; stateful or hardto-partition workloads. Beyond one machine, or HA needed; stateless or partitionable. R U L E Scale up first if it is cheap; plan the way out. SCALE & OPS Active–passive vs Active–active Active–passive Active–active Simpler; failover time is acceptable. Near-zero downtime, regional load sharing; conflict handling in place. R U L E Active-active costs data and routing complexity. SCALE & OPS Multi-AZ vs Multi-region Multi-AZ Multi-region Default high availability within one region. Regional-outage RTO, latency to users, data residency. R U L E Multi-region only when the business case is explicit. SCALE & OPS Managed service vs Self-hosted Managed Self-hosted Small team; commodity capability; time matters. Cost at large scale, deep tuning, compliance or portability needs. R U L E Run it yourself only if it is core to your edge. SCALE & OPS Build vs Buy Build Buy Core differentiator; unique requirements; long horizon. Commodity capability; speed matters; vendor fits well. R U L E Buy the commodity, build the differentiator. SCALE & OPS Blocking + virtual threads vs Reactive Virtual threads Reactive Simple code, I/O-bound services; readable stack traces. Streaming pipelines needing backpressure and composition. R U L E On modern Java, try virtual threads first. Deploy DEPLOY Rolling vs Blue-green vs Canary Rolling Blue-green Cheap; tolerates Instant rollback; mixed versions needs double briefly. capacity and DB compatibility. Canary Limits blast radius with real traffic; needs metrics and routing. R U L E Canary for risky changes; rolling for routine ones. THE RULE Name the problem, check the constraints, pick the simpler option, and write the revisit trigger into an ADR.

INSIDE Eight steps with a 45-minute plan Estimation recipe and numbers to remember Scaling ladder and deep-dive menu Question bank and common failures THE PLAN REFERENCE SKELETON Eight steps, 45 minutes Most systems are a variation of this STEP WHAT TIME 1 Clarify requirements 5 min 2 Estimate 4 min 3 API and data model 6 min 4 High-level design 10 min 5 Deep dives 12 min 6 Failure and reliability 4 min 7 Operations and security 2 min 8 Wrap up 2 min Clients ↓ DNS + CDN ↓ Load balancer ↓ API gateway auth · rate limit ↓ Stateless services scale horizontally A repeatable flow. Adapt the order to the interviewer, and check in at the end of each step. ↓ Cache · Primary DB + replicas · Object storage read path and write path ↓ Queue / log → Workers async work, spikes, fan-out ↓ Search · analytics · notifications derived views The eight steps STEP 1 · 5 MIN Clarify requirements DO Ask for the 3–4 core features, then what is out of scope. Pin down non-functionals: scale, read/write ratio, latency, availability, consistency, retention, regions. PRODUCE Written functional and non-functional lists, agreed with the interviewer. AVOID Assuming scale. Designing before scope is agreed. STEP 2 · 4 MIN Estimate DO DAU → average QPS → peak QPS. Storage per year. Bandwidth. Cache size. State every assumption aloud and round hard. PRODUCE Four or five numbers that drive later choices (e.g. read QPS decides caching). AVOID False precision. Numbers that never influence the design. STEP 3 · 6 MIN API and data model DO 3–5 endpoints: verb, path, key params. Idempotency key on writes. Pagination on lists. Entities, keys and indexes taken from the access patterns. Choose the store per entity. PRODUCE Endpoint list and a table or key sketch per entity. AVOID A schema with no query behind it. STEP 4 · 10 MIN High-level design DO Draw the skeleton first, then specialise it. Walk the write path and the read path end to end. Name the store for each entity. PRODUCE A box diagram with labelled flows, readable from across the table. AVOID Technology names with no stated role. Boxes you cannot justify. STEP 5 · 12 MIN Deep dives DO Pick the 2–3 hardest parts, or follow the interviewer's lead. For each: the bottleneck, two options, the numbers, the choice, the cost. PRODUCE Decisions with reasons, not just components. AVOID Skimming five topics instead of owning two. STEP 6 · 4 MIN Failure and reliability DO Find single points of failure. Replication and failover. Retries with backoff plus idempotency. Dead-letter queue. Degrade gracefully. State RPO and RTO if data matters. PRODUCE A short list of failure scenarios and what the user experiences in each. AVOID Describing only the happy path. STEP 7 · 2 MIN Operations and security DO Metrics and SLOs, alerts, tracing. Authentication, authorisation, rate limiting, PII handling. Name the main cost driver. PRODUCE Three or four lines, each tied to this system. AVOID A generic checklist unrelated to the design. STEP 8 · 2 MIN Wrap up DO Restate the key decisions and their trade-offs. What breaks at 10× scale, and what you would build next. PRODUCE A confident 30-second summary. AVOID Trailing off. Introducing new components at the end. 04 04 Spring Boot Internals How the context starts, how auto-configuration and proxies work, and why annotations silently fail. INSIDE Startup sequence and bean lifecycle Proxies and @Transactional pitfalls Config, async, data, security, testing “Why isn't it working?” table SCOPE About these notes Assumes Spring Boot 3.x and Java 17+ . Check names and defaults against your versions. THE KEY IDEA Most Spring surprises come from two facts: beans are created and wired by the container, and cross-cutting behaviour is added by proxies. If a call bypasses the container or the proxy, the annotation does nothing. Startup STARTUP SEQUENCE Where auto-configuration and proxies enter SpringApplication.run ↓ Prepare Environment ↓ Create ApplicationContext ↓ Load definitions scan + auto-configuration ↓ Post-process factory post-processors ↓ Create beans DI · BeanPostProcessors · proxies ↓ Start embedded server Tomcat and friends ↓ Runners + ApplicationReadyEvent Auto-configuration is applied while definitions load. Proxies for @Transactional, @Async and @Cacheable are created when beans are post-processed. STARTUP @SpringBootApplication Combines @Configuration , @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan . Component scan covers the main class's package and below. Beans outside it are not found. Auto-configuration classes are listed in META- INF/spring/…AutoConfiguration.imports . Conditions decide what applies: @ConditionalOnClass , @ConditionalOnMissingBean , @ConditionalOnProperty . Start with --debug to print the condition evaluation report. Beans BEANS Bean lifecycle Instantiate (constructor) Inject dependencies Aware callbacks BeanPostProcessor before-init @PostConstruct , InitializingBean, init-method BeanPostProcessor after-init (proxies created here) Ready for use @PreDestroy , DisposableBean on shutdown BEANS Injection and scopes Singleton Default. One shared instance; must be thread-safe Prototype New instance per injection or lookup Request / session Web-scoped; need a scoped proxy when injected into a singleton Prefer constructor injection : immutable, testable, fails fast. Circular dependencies are rejected by default since Boot 2.6. Fix the design. Use @Primary or @Qualifier for several candidates. Proxies PROXIES How proxies work Spring AOP wraps beans in proxies: JDK interface proxies or CGLIB class proxies (CGLIB is the Boot default). Calls through the proxy get the advice: transactions, async, caching, security. A call from inside the same object skips the proxy ( self- invocation). Private and final methods cannot be proxied by CGLIB. Fix: move the method to another bean, inject the proxied bean, or use AspectJ weaving. WHY IT BREAKS this.method() never goes through the proxy. That is why so many annotations “do nothing”. PROXIES @Transactional pitfalls Self-invocation or a non-Spring-managed object: no transaction. By default rolls back on unchecked exceptions and Errors only; set rollbackFor for checked ones. Swallowing the exception inside the method prevents rollback. REQUIRED joins an existing transaction; REQUIRES_NEW suspends it and starts another. readOnly is a hint to the driver and ORM, not a guarantee. @Async and new threads do not inherit the transaction. Lazy loading outside a transaction throws LazyInitializationException . Keep the boundary at the service layer and keep it short. Web and config W E B Request flow Servlet filters ↓ DispatcherServlet HandlerMapping ↓ Interceptors preHandle ↓ Argument resolvers @RequestBody, @Valid ↓ Controller ↓ HttpMessageConverter ↓ Interceptors postHandle Exceptions go to @ControllerAdvice . ProblemDetail gives standard error bodies (Spring 6 / Boot 3). Validate at the edge with @Valid and constraint annotations. CONFIG Configuration Precedence, roughly: command-line args, environment variables, profile files, application.yml , defaults. Prefer @ConfigurationProperties (typed, validated with @Validated ) over scattered @Value . Relaxed binding maps MY_APP_PORT to my.app.port . Profiles select environment config; do not commit secrets. @RefreshScope (Spring Cloud) rebinds on refresh. ASYNC Async, scheduling and threads @Async needs @EnableAsync , and goes through the proxy. Define your own executor; the defaults may not suit load. Exceptions in void async methods are lost without a handler. @Scheduled runs on a single thread by default; use a distributed lock (such as ShedLock) when scaling out. Boot 3.2+ on Java 21: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true uses virtual threads. Verify against your versions. Data and security D ATA Data access HikariCP is the default pool; tune maximum-pool-size by measurement. spring.jpa.open-in-view defaults to true. Consider disabling it to avoid lazy loading in the view layer. Use Flyway or Liquibase for migrations. Watch for N+1 queries; check generated SQL. @Transactional(readOnly = true) for query services. SECURITY Spring Security Register a SecurityFilterChain bean; WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter is gone in Spring Security 6. Filter chain order matters; authentication runs before authorization. Method security needs @EnableMethodSecurity . Stateless APIs: validate JWTs with the resource server support. CSRF protection is for browser sessions; know when to disable it. 05 05 Database Essentials Indexing, query plans, isolation and locking, ORM pitfalls, pagination, schema design, scaling and migrations. INSIDE Index rules and query plans Isolation levels and locking N+1, pagination and schema design Scaling ladder, migrations, MongoDB THE HABIT Measure before tuning THE HABIT Read the query plan, check the index, shorten the transaction, then scale. Most database incidents are one of those four. For backend engineers working with MySQL, PostgreSQL and MongoDB. Indexes and queries INDEXES Indexing rules B-tree indexes serve equality, range and ordering on the leading columns. Composite index: order columns by equality first, then range ; the leftmost-prefix rule applies. Covering index: the query is answered from the index alone. Functions on the column ( LOWER(col) ) or a leading wildcard ( LIKE '%x' ) defeat a normal index. Implicit type conversion can silently skip an index. Every index slows writes and uses space. Drop unused ones. Low-cardinality columns alone are poor indexes. QUERIES Reading a query plan Run EXPLAIN (and EXPLAIN ANALYZE where available). Red flags: full scan on a large table, a sort on disk, temporary tables, rows examined far above rows returned. Stale statistics mislead the planner; refresh them ( ANALYZE ). Fix the query and index first, hints last. EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ... FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20; QUERIES Pagination Offset Simple, but cost grows with depth; unstable if rows change Keyset (seek) Stable and fast. Needs a unique, indexed sort key. WHERE (created_at, id) Return a cursor, not a page number, for large feeds. Transactions TRANSACTIONS Isolation levels Read uncommitted Dirty reads possible Read committed No dirty reads. Non-repeatable reads and phantoms possible Repeatable read Stable reads in a transaction. Behaviour on phantoms differs by engine Serializable As if run one at a time. Most conflicts and retries Common defaults: MySQL InnoDB uses repeatable read; PostgreSQL uses read committed. Snapshot-style repeatable read can still allow write skew. Higher isolation costs throughput; handle serialization failures with retries. TRANSACTIONS Locking and concurrency Optimistic : a version column and a conditional update. Best with low contention. Pessimistic : SELECT … FOR UPDATE . Best when conflicts are frequent. SKIP LOCKED lets workers claim rows without blocking (PostgreSQL and MySQL 8). Avoid deadlocks: lock in a consistent order and keep transactions short. Never hold a transaction open across a remote call. Make writes idempotent so retries are safe. O R M N+1 and ORM pitfalls Symptom: one query for the list, then one per row. Fix: fetch join, @EntityGraph , batch fetching, or a DTO projection. Lazy loading outside a transaction throws LazyInitializationException . Avoid returning entities from APIs; return DTOs. Set ddl-auto to none or validate in production; use Flyway or Liquibase. Log SQL and count statements in tests for hot paths. Design and scale DESIGN Schema design Normalise by default; denormalise deliberately for proven read paths. Money: DECIMAL or integer minor units, never floating point. Store timestamps in UTC. Random UUIDs fragment B-tree indexes; time-ordered IDs (UUIDv7, ULID, snowflake) insert more smoothly. Soft deletes complicate uniqueness and queries; weigh the cost. Add foreign-key indexes where you join or delete. SCALE Scaling ladder Fix queries and indexes Tune connection pooling Cache hot reads Read replicas (mind replication lag) Archive or partition large tables Shard by a well-chosen key Replica reads can be stale; route read-your-writes traffic to the primary. SCALE Connection pools The pool should be small and sized by measurement. HikariCP's pool-sizing guidance explains why far fewer connections often perform better. Total connections across all instances must fit the server's limit. Watch pool wait time as an early warning. CONSISTENCY Replication and consistency Async replication Fast writes; replicas can lag; failover can lose recent writes Sync replication No loss on failover; higher write latency Read-your-writes Route a user's reads to the primary shortly after a write Failover Automate, fence the old primary, test regularly CACHING Caching with a database Cache-aside is the default: read, miss, load, store. Set TTLs; decide how invalidation happens on writes. Protect hot keys from stampedes with locking or early refresh. Cache the result of expensive queries, not everything. The database remains the source of truth. PARTITIONING Partitioning vs sharding Partitioning Split a table inside one database: prune scans, drop old data cheaply Sharding Split data across servers: scales writes and storage, adds complexity Shard key High cardinality, even load, matches common queries Cross-shard joins and transactions are the cost. SQL, change and documents S Q L Features worth knowing CTEs and window functions ( ROW_NUMBER , LAG , running totals). JOIN types, and when an anti-join ( NOT EXISTS ) is clearer than NOT IN . Upsert: INSERT … ON CONFLICT (PostgreSQL) or ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE (MySQL). Partial and functional indexes where supported. JSON columns for flexible attributes; index the fields you filter on. Bulk operations and batching instead of row-by-row loops. CHANGE Safe migrations Expand, migrate, contract : add, backfill in small batches, switch, then drop. Check how your engine's DDL locks the table before running it on production. Keep schema and code deployable in either order. Test rollbacks and keep backups current. MONGODB Document-store essentials Model by access pattern: embed data read together; reference when it grows without bound or is shared. Compound index order: Equality, Sort, Range. Shard key needs high cardinality and even distribution; avoid monotonically increasing keys. Choose read and write concerns to match durability needs. Documents have a size limit; avoid unbounded arrays. OPERATIONS Backup and recovery Define RPO and RTO first. Point-in-time recovery needs continuous log archiving. A backup you have not restored is a hope, not a backup. Test restores on a schedule. PITFALLS Common mistakes SELECT * on wide tables. Missing index on a foreign key or a filter column. OR conditions and huge IN lists that skip indexes. COUNT(*) on very large tables on a hot path. Long transactions and idle-in-transaction sessions. Treating the cache as the source of truth. Running migrations that lock a busy table. THE RULE Measure before tuning: read the plan, check the index, shorten the transaction, then scale.

06 06 Caching Cheat Sheet Where to cache, which pattern to pick, how to invalidate, how caches fail under load, and the Redis and Spring settings that matter. INSIDE Layers and six caching strategies Invalidation and the races to know Stampede, penetration, avalanche, hot key Redis structures, locks, rate limits, Spring Layers from user to database Browser HTTP cache: max-age, ETag ↓ CDN edge cache for static and public content ↓ API gateway response cache, rarely needed ↓ Service · L1 in-process Caffeine, microseconds ↓ Redis · L2 distributed shared, about 1 ms ↓ Database source of truth: buffer pool, milliseconds Each layer cuts latency and load, and adds one more place for stale data. Latencies are typical orders of magnitude. Where and how LAYERS Where to cache Browser / HTTP Static assets, GET responses with Cache- Control. Free, zero network. CDN Public, shared content close to users. Offloads origin. In-process (L1) Caffeine. Fastest, but per instance: copies diverge, no shared invalidation. Distributed (L2) Redis or Memcached. Shared across instances, network hop, own failure modes. Database Buffer pool, query plans, read replicas. Tune before adding another layer. PATTERNS Caching strategies Cache-aside App reads cache, on miss loads DB and fills. Default choice. Risk: stale data, stampede. Read-through Cache loads from DB itself. Simpler app code, needs a loader. Write-through Write cache and DB together. Fresh reads, slower writes. Write-behind Write cache, flush to DB later. Fast writes, can lose data on crash. Write-around Write DB only, cache fills on read. Good for write-once, rarely-read data. Refresh-ahead Reload hot keys before expiry. Smooth latency, wasted work on cold keys. DESIGN Cache key design Pattern: service:entity:id:v3 . Include tenant, locale and version when they change the value. Keep keys short and readable; hash long query strings. Never put secrets or raw PII in keys. Namespace by environment so test and prod never collide. Cache DTOs, not JPA entities. Make values immutable and serialisable. Version the value schema so a deploy does not read old shapes. Freshness FRESHNESS Invalidation TTL is the safety net. Always set one, and add random jitter (±10–20%). Delete on write , do not update: the next read refills. Updating the cache from a write path invites race conditions. Event-driven : publish change events (outbox, CDC) and evict in every consumer. Best for multi-service caches. Versioned keys ( product:42:v7 ): never invalidate, old keys expire. Tag or prefix groups for bulk eviction, via a set of keys per tag. Know your staleness budget per data type: price and stock differ from a profile photo. THE RACE TO KNOW Reader misses and loads the old row, writer updates the DB and deletes the key, reader then writes the old value into the cache. Fix with short TTL, versioned keys, or a delayed second delete. FAILURE MODES Symptom → cause → fix Stampede Hot key expires, many requests hit the DB. Single-flight lock, early probabilistic refresh, stale-while-revalidate. Penetration Requests for keys that never exist. Cache the negative result with a short TTL, or use a Bloom filter. Avalanche Many keys expire together. TTL jitter, staggered warm-up. Hot key One key saturates a shard. Put L1 in front, or replicate the key with suffixes k#1..k#N . Big key A large value blocks the single-threaded server. Split, compress, use hash fields. Cache down DB overload. Circuit breaker, bulkhead, load shedding, degrade gracefully. Cold start After deploy or failover. Pre-warm hot keys, ramp traffic. Memory and Redis MEMORY Eviction policies LRU Drops the least recently used. Good default. LFU Drops the least frequently used. Resists one-off scans. TTL Expires by time. Always combine with a size limit. Caffeine Window TinyLFU: near-optimal hit rate, bounded size. maxmemory 2gb maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru # allkeys-lfu · volatile-lru # volatile-ttl · noeviction (default) With noeviction, writes fail when memory is full. Cache workloads normally want allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu. REDIS Pick the data structure String Values, counters (INCR), locks (SET NX EX). Hash Object fields, partial updates. List Queues, recent items. Set / ZSet Tags and uniqueness. ZSet: leaderboards, rate-limit windows, delayed jobs. Stream Log with consumer groups. Use Kafka when durability and scale matter. Bitmap / HLL Flags per user, approximate unique counts. REDIS Deployment topologies Standalone Dev and small caches. Single point of failure. Sentinel Primary plus replicas with automatic failover. One shard only. Cluster 16384 hash slots sharded across nodes. Multi-key commands need the same slot (hash tags like {user42} ). Persistence RDB and AOF are optional. Replication is async: a failover can lose recent writes. REDIS Sizing a cache Estimate: items × (average value size + per-key overhead) × replication factor. Leave headroom for fragmentation, replication buffers and fork copy-on-write; do not run maxmemory at 100% of RAM. Hit ratio depends on skew: a small hot set gives a high ratio from a small cache. Measure hit ratio at two cache sizes before buying more memory. Patterns with Redis PATTERN Distributed lock: know the limits SET lock:order:42 token NX PX 30000 # release only if the token matches # (use a Lua script: GET, compare, DEL) The lease can expire during a long GC pause or slow call while you still think you hold the lock. For correctness, use a fencing token checked by the resource, or a database constraint. Use Redis locks for efficiency (avoid duplicate work), not as the only safety net. PATTERN Rate limiting with Redis Fixed window INCR a key per window, EXPIRE. Simple; allows bursts at the boundary. Sliding window ZSET of timestamps, trim then count. Accurate, more memory. Token bucket Refill rate plus capacity, via a Lua script. Smooth, burst-friendly. Make the check-and-update atomic with a Lua script or a single command; two round trips race. EXAMPLE Worked example: product catalogue Read-heavy, tolerates a little staleness: cache-aside. L1 Caffeine, 30 s TTL, plus L2 Redis, 10 min TTL with jitter. Price change event (outbox, Kafka) evicts the key in both layers. Stock level: not cached, or a very short TTL, because correctness matters. Single-flight loading on miss to stop stampedes on popular items. Dashboards: hit ratio, p99 with and without cache, eviction rate. In Spring and HTTP SPRING Spring Boot caching @EnableCaching @Cacheable(cacheNames = "products", key = "#id", sync = true) Product get(long id) { ... } @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "products", key = "#p.id") void update(Product p) { ... } # application.yml spring.cache.type: caffeine spring.cache.caffeine.spec: > maximumSize=10000, expireAfterWrite=10m Annotations work through proxies: self-invocation and private methods bypass the cache. sync=true stops a stampede only within one JVM. Redis: set spring.cache.redis.time-to-live or configure RedisCacheManager with per-cache TTL. H T T P HTTP caching headers max-age / s- Freshness for browser / shared caches. maxage no-cache Store, but revalidate every time. no-store Never store (sensitive data). ETag + If-None- Conditional GET; the server answers 304. Match stale-while- Serve stale while refreshing in the revalidate background. Vary Headers that change the response (Accept-Encoding, Authorization). C L I Redis commands redis-cli INFO stats # hits, misses redis-cli --bigkeys redis-cli --hotkeys # needs LFU policy MEMORY USAGE key SLOWLOG GET 10 SCAN 0 MATCH user:* COUNT 100 TTL key Never run KEYS * in production: it blocks the server. Use SCAN. MEASURE What to watch Hit ratio per cache, not global p99 latency with and without the cache Eviction rate and memory used Miss penalty (cost of the DB load) Connection pool and timeouts to Redis Stale-data incidents WHEN NOT TO CACHE Do not cache when data changes on every read, the hit rate stays low, or correctness needs strong consistency. THE RULE A cache is a copy, and every copy can be wrong. Decide the staleness you accept, set a TTL, protect the database from stampedes, and measure the hit ratio before and after.

07 07 Kafka Cheat Sheet The model, the guarantees, the settings that matter, the failure modes and the commands. INSIDE Partitions, replicas, consumer groups Delivery semantics and the durability recipe Producer and consumer settings Failure modes and CLI commands Kafka in one picture Producers key → partition ↓ Topic: orders (3 partitions, RF = 3) P0 · P1 · P2, each an ordered append-only log ↓ Consumer group: payments one partition → one consumer in the group ↓ Offsets committed per partition lag = log-end offset − committed offset THE RULE Kafka is a distributed log. Ordering lives in a partition, parallelism is the partition count, durability comes from replication, and delivery guarantees come from when you commit. Concepts MODEL Core concepts Topic Named stream of records Partition Ordered, append-only log; unit of parallelism and ordering Offset Position of a record within a partition Broker Server storing partitions Replica / ISR Leader plus followers; ISR = in-sync replicas Consumer group Members split a topic's partitions; each partition goes to one member Lag Log-end offset minus committed offset Controller KRaft quorum manages metadata (ZooKeeper removed in Kafka 4.0) MODEL Ordering and partitioning Order is guaranteed only within a partition. The record key picks the partition, so one key keeps its order. Maximum consumer parallelism in a group = partition count. Adding partitions changes the key → partition mapping for new records. A skewed key creates a hot partition. Pick the key for ordering needs first, then check the distribution. Guarantees GUARANTEES Delivery semantics At most once Commit offset, then process. Can lose messages At least once Process, then commit. Can duplicate. The usual default Exactly once Idempotent producer + transactions + read_committed, inside Kafka. Outside Kafka, make the sink idempotent ALWAYS Design consumers to be idempotent regardless. GUARANTEES Durability recipe replication.factor=3 min.insync.replicas=2 acks=all enable.idempotence=true unclean.leader.election.enable=false With acks=all , a write succeeds only if at least min.insync.replicas replicas have it. Idempotence is on by default in recent clients; make it explicit. One broker can fail with no loss and no write outage. Configuration CONFIG Producer settings acks 0, 1 or all. Durability vs latency linger.ms / Batching: throughput vs latency batch.size compression.type lz4 or zstd cut bytes and cost retries / Total time budget for a send delivery.timeout.ms max.in.flight.requests ≤ 5 keeps order with idempotence on buffer.memory Producer buffer; send blocks when full CONFIG Consumer settings enable.auto.commit Prefer false; commit after processing auto.offset.reset earliest or latest when no offset exists max.poll.records Batch size per poll max.poll.interval.ms Exceed it and the member is kicked out, triggering a rebalance session.timeout.ms Missed heartbeats evict a member isolation.level read_committed to skip aborted transactions group.instance.id Static membership; fewer rebalances on restart Operations OPERATIONS Rebalances and lag Triggers: member joins or leaves, session timeout, poll interval exceeded, partition change. Use the cooperative sticky assignor to avoid stop-theworld rebalances. Use static membership for rolling restarts. Keep per-poll processing well under max.poll.interval.ms . Lag rising means consumers are slower than producers, or are stuck in rebalance loops. Scale consumers only up to the partition count. PATTERNS Reliability patterns Transactional outbox for DB write + publish atomically. Idempotent consumer : dedupe on a business key. Retry topics with delays, then a dead-letter topic. Handle poison messages: tolerant deserializers, DLQ, alert. Backpressure with pause and resume. Spring Kafka: DefaultErrorHandler with backoff, DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer , @RetryableTopic . STORAGE Retention and compaction delete policy Drop old segments by retention.ms or retention.bytes compact policy Keep the latest record per key; null value = tombstone segment.bytes Segment size; affects cleanup granularity Disk estimate throughput × retention × replication factor Tiered storage depends on your Kafka version and vendor; check before relying on it. D ATA Schemas and compatibility Use a schema registry with Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema. Modes: BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL (plus transitive variants). Add optional fields with defaults. Never reuse a field number or change a type. Version event names and keep consumers tolerant of unknown fields. Troubleshooting DEBUG Symptom → cause → check Lag growing Slow consumer, few partitions, rebalance loop. Describe the group Duplicates At-least-once, rebalance before commit. Add idempotency Lost messages acks=1, unclean election, commit before processing Out of order No key, or retries with in-flight > 1 and no idempotence Frequent Poll interval exceeded, GC pauses, rebalances flapping pods Producer timeouts ISR below min.insync.replicas, broker down, network Under-replicated Slow or down broker; check broker health partitions and disk One busy partition Skewed key; change the key or add a salt C L I Commands # BS = --bootstrap-server h:9092 kafka-topics.sh $BS --create \ --topic t --partitions 6 \ --replication-factor 3 kafka-topics.sh $BS \ --describe --topic t kafka-console-consumer.sh $BS \ --topic t --from-beginning kafka-consumer-groups.sh $BS \ --describe --group g kafka-consumer-groups.sh $BS \ --group g --topic t \ --reset-offsets --to-earliest \ --execute Resetting offsets needs the group to be inactive. Run without --execute first to preview. SIZING Partitions and capacity Partitions ≈ target throughput ÷ measured per-partition throughput, on the producer and consumer side. Take the larger. More partitions mean more open files, slower recovery and longer rebalances. Plan for future consumer parallelism; you cannot reduce partitions. Use RF 3 across zones for production topics. F I T Kafka or not Use for Replayable event log, many consumers, high throughput, stream processing, CDC Avoid for Per-message routing and priority, lowvolume task queues, request-reply Operating Kafka is a team cost; weigh managed offerings. OBSERVE What to monitor Consumer lag per group and partition Under-replicated and offline partitions ISR shrink rate Request latency and error rate Disk usage and retention headroom Producer retry and error rates Rebalance frequency Kafka Connect Kafka Streams ksqlDB Schema Registry MirrorMaker 2 TLS + SASL ACLs Quotas Ordering lives in a partition, parallelism is the partition count, durability comes from replication, and delivery guarantees come from when you commit.

08 08 Service Communication Decisions How services should talk: sync or async, which protocol, which broker, how to keep calls safe, and how to change contracts without breaking anyone. INSIDE Sync or async decision flow REST, gRPC, GraphQL, queues, logs Saga, outbox, idempotency keys Timeouts, retries, breakers, contracts DECISION FLOW Sync or async first Does the caller need the answer now? ↓ YES → Synchronous REST for public and partners · gRPC for hot internal paths · GraphQL for flexible client queries ↓ NO → Asynchronous Queue for work · event log for facts · saga for long workflows DEFAULT Default: REST between teams and to the outside, gRPC for hot internal paths, events to tell other domains what happened. Keep the sync call chain shallow. Pick a protocol SYNCHRONOUS REST, gRPC, GraphQL and friends REST / JSON Public and partner APIs, CRUD, broad tooling. Avoid for high-volume internal calls and streaming. gRPC Internal, low latency, strong contracts, streaming. Avoid for browsers without a proxy and ad hoc debugging. GraphQL Many clients need different shapes. Avoid for simple CRUD; watch N+1 and query cost. WebSocket Two-way, low latency (chat, trading). Stateful: needs sticky routing and a scaling plan. SSE Server-to-client stream over HTTP. Simple, auto-reconnect. Webhook Notify an external system. Needs signatures, retries, idempotency. ASYNCHRONOUS Queue, log or pub/sub Queue RabbitMQ, SQS. One consumer per message, ack and delete, work distribution, flexible routing. Log Kafka. Retained and replayable, ordering per partition, many independent consumers. Pub/sub SNS, Redis pub/sub. Fan-out, fire and forget; check the durability guarantee. COMPARE If this, then that SITUATION PICK Browser or partner calls us REST Service-to-service, high QPS gRPC Mobile app needs a custom shape GraphQL or BFF Do work later, one worker Queue Many services react to a fact Event log / pub-sub Live updates to the browser SSE or WebSocket Tell an external customer Webhook Multi-step business process Saga Messages and workflows MESSAGES Command, event, query Command Do this. One receiver, may be rejected. Imperative name: ReserveStock . Event This happened. Immutable, many listeners. Past tense: OrderPlaced . Query Give me data. Synchronous, no side effects. Event notification : small, consumers call back for details. Low coupling, more calls. Event-carried state : the event holds the data. Consumers stay autonomous, schema coupling grows. WORKFLOWS Orchestration vs choreography Orchestration A central coordinator tells each step. Visible flow, easy to change; the coordinator is a coupling point. Choreography Services react to events. Loose coupling, hard to see the whole flow. A distributed transaction is a saga: local transactions plus compensating actions. Avoid 2PC across services in most systems. EXAMPLE Saga: place an order 1 · Create order status PENDING ↓ 2 · Reserve stock compensation: release stock ↓ 3 · Charge payment compensation: refund ↓ 4 · Confirm order status CONFIRMED If step 3 fails, run compensations in reverse order and mark the order FAILED. Every step and compensation must be idempotent and retryable. Persist saga state so a crash can resume. DELIVERY Guarantees and idempotency Networks give at-least-once: design every handler to be idempotent. Idempotency key per request, or dedupe on a business key. Transactional outbox : write state and event in one DB transaction, relay to the broker. Order matters only per key: partition by that key. Poison messages: bounded retries, then a dead-letter queue and an alert. PATTERN Idempotency key flow Client sends Idempotency-Key: uuid with the write. Server stores key, request hash and result in one transaction. A repeat with the same key returns the stored result. Same key with a different body is rejected (409/422). Keys expire after a retention window. PATTERN Transactional outbox In one DB transaction: update the entity and insert an outbox row. A relay (poller or CDC) reads new rows and publishes to the broker. Mark rows sent, or delete them, after publish. Consumers dedupe, because the relay is at-least-once. This closes the gap between “saved to DB” and “event published”. Make every call safe RESILIENCE Every remote call needs Timeout Always set. The caller's deadline is shorter than its own caller's. Retry Idempotent calls only, exponential backoff with jitter, bounded. Circuit breaker Stop calling a failing dependency, fail fast, probe to recover. Bulkhead Separate pools per dependency so one cannot starve the rest. Fallback Cached or degraded answer, when acceptable. RETRY AMPLIFICATION 3 layers each retrying 3 times means up to 27 calls on the failing service. Retry at one layer and propagate deadlines. BUDGET Timeout budget example client 2000 ms gateway 1800 ms service A 1500 ms service B 1000 ms database 500 ms Each hop gets less time than its caller. gRPC propagates deadlines natively; for HTTP, pass a deadline header. CONFIG Resilience4j starter config resilience4j: circuitbreaker.instances.payments: slidingWindowSize: 20 failureRateThreshold: 50 waitDurationInOpenState: 30s retry.instances.payments: maxAttempts: 3 waitDuration: 200ms enableExponentialBackoff: true Tune to measured behaviour. Add jitter and a retry budget where supported. Contracts and API design EVOLUTION Change without breaking Safe: add optional fields. Unsafe: remove, rename, retype, change meaning. Consumers ignore unknown fields ( tolerant reader). Version only for breaking changes (path /v2 or a header). Run both versions during migration. Contract tests (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract) catch breaks in CI. Messages: schema registry with backward or full compatibility. G R P C What to know Four call types: unary, server stream, client stream, bidirectional. Always set a deadline ; it propagates down the call chain. Protobuf: never reuse or renumber a field; add new fields only. Long-lived HTTP/2 connections: use client-side or L7 load balancing. API DESIGN Checklist for a good HTTP API Cursor pagination on lists Consistent error body (RFC 9457 problem details) 429 with Retry-After for rate limits Idempotency keys on unsafe writes Versioning and deprecation policy Timeouts documented and enforced Authentication on every route OpenAPI spec kept in CI Spring toolkit and network SPRING Toolkit REST client RestClient (6.1+), WebClient for reactive, @HttpExchange interfaces Resilience Resilience4j: @CircuitBreaker , @Retry , @Bulkhead , @TimeLimiter Edge Spring Cloud Gateway Messaging Spring Kafka, Spring AMQP, Spring Cloud Stream Contracts Spring Cloud Contract, OpenAPI RestClient c = RestClient.builder() .baseUrl(url) .requestFactory(factory) // set timeouts .build(); NETWORK Discovery, load balancing, security Kubernetes Service DNS covers most discovery; a mesh adds mTLS, retries and traffic shifting. gRPC keeps long-lived HTTP/2 connections: an L4 load balancer pins them to one pod. Use client-side or L7 balancing. Authenticate services: mTLS or OAuth2 client credentials. Propagate the user's identity token only when needed. Gateway for north-south traffic, mesh or direct calls for east-west. SMELLS Common mistakes Distributed monolith : services deploy together or share a database. Chatty calls and deep sync chains: latency multiplies, availability multiplies down. No timeouts or unbounded retries. Events that are really commands in disguise. Breaking a contract without a version or contract test. Choose the weakest coupling that meets the requirement. Ask whether the caller must wait; if not, publish an event. Always set timeouts and make handlers idempotent.

10 10 Observability Cheat Sheet What to instrument, how to alert, how to trace a request across services, and how to go from an alert to a cause. INSIDE Signals, RED, USE, SLOs and burn-rate alerts Metrics, structured logs, traces Spring Boot, OpenTelemetry, PromQL, LogQL Triage flow, dashboards and cost control THE PIPELINE From service to on-call Spring Boot services Micrometer + OpenTelemetry ↓ OTel Collector receive · batch · sample ↓ Prometheus · Loki · Tempo metrics · logs · traces ↓ Grafana dashboards and explore, one traceId across all three ↓ Alertmanager route · dedupe ↓ On-call with a runbook I D E A One traceId links all three signals: metric exemplar → trace → logs. Collect once with OpenTelemetry, store in the backend you choose. Concepts CONCEPTS Signals and questions Metrics Is something wrong, and how bad? Cheap numbers over time. Alerts and trends. Logs What exactly happened? Events with context. Expensive at volume. Traces Where did the time go across services? One request, many spans. Profiles Which code burns CPU or memory? Continuous profiling. Events What changed? Deploys, flags, config. Overlay on dashboards. METHOD Golden signals, RED, USE Golden signals Latency, traffic, errors, saturation. Every service. RED Rate, Errors, Duration. For request-driven services. USE Utilization, Saturation, Errors. For resources: CPU, pool, disk, queue. Start with RED per endpoint and USE per resource (JVM heap, Hikari pool, thread pool, Kafka lag). RELIABILITY SLI, SLO, error budget SLI: good events ÷ valid events (e.g. requests under 300 ms that are not 5xx). SLO: target for the SLI over a window (99.9% over 30 days). Error budget = 1 − SLO. 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of bad time per 30 days. Budget burning fast: freeze risky releases, fix reliability first. 99% ~7.2 hours / 30 days 99.9% ~43 minutes / 30 days 99.99% ~4.3 minutes / 30 days Alerting ALERTING Alert on symptoms and burn rate Page on user pain (errors, latency, SLO burn), not on causes (CPU 80%). Every page is urgent, actionable and links a runbook. Multi-window burn rate (30-day SLO): page at 14.4× over 1 h and 5 min; page at 6× over 6 h; ticket at 1× over 3 days. Route by severity: page, ticket, or dashboard only. Delete alerts nobody acts on. T E S T If an alert fires and the response is “wait and see”, it is not a page. ALERTING Prometheus alert rule example - alert: HighErrorRatio expr: | sum(rate( http_server_requests_seconds_count {status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate( http_server_requests_seconds_count [5m])) > 0.02 for: 5m labels: {severity: page} annotations: runbook_url: https://runbooks/x Prefer SLO burn-rate rules for paging; use simple thresholds for tickets. Metrics, logs, traces METRICS Types and cardinality Counter Only goes up. Use rate(). Requests, errors. Gauge Goes up and down. Queue size, heap. Histogram Buckets, aggregatable across instances. Use for latency. Summary Client-side quantiles, cannot be aggregated. Never average percentiles. Aggregate histogram buckets, then compute the quantile. Labels multiply series. No user IDs, request IDs or raw URLs as labels. METRICS Business metrics with Micrometer Counter.builder("orders.placed") .tag("channel", "web") .register(registry) .increment(); Timer t = Timer.builder("payment.latency") .publishPercentileHistogram() .register(registry); t.record(() -> charge(order)); Count things the business cares about, not only HTTP. L O G S Structured logging JSON, one event per line, fixed field names. Always include traceId , spanId , service, version, level. Log decisions and failures, not every step. No PII, tokens or secrets. Log once at the boundary where the error is handled, not at every layer. Sample or drop DEBUG in production. Spring Boot 3.4+: logging.structured.format.console=ecs . L O G S Log levels ERROR Needs a human or a fix. Should be rare and actionable. WARN Unexpected but handled. Watch the trend. INFO Business events and lifecycle. Default in production. DEBUG Developer detail. Off in production, switchable at runtime. TRACING Context propagation and sampling traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736 -00f067aa0ba902b7-01 ver · trace id (32 hex) · span id (16 hex) · flags W3C traceparent is the standard header. Propagate it through HTTP and Kafka/AMQP headers. Head sampling : decide at start, cheap, may miss rare errors. Tail sampling : decide after the trace ends (keep errors and slow ones). Runs in the collector. Async hops and thread pools lose context unless wrapped. ASYNC Tracing Kafka and async work Propagate trace context in message headers. Spring Kafka (Boot 3.2+): enable spring.kafka.template.observation-enabled and spring.kafka.listener.observation-enabled . Link consumer spans to the producer span so a trace crosses the broker. Wrap custom executors so context follows the thread. Run it TRIAGE Alert to root cause Open the RED dashboard for the service. Check what changed: deploy, flag, config. Follow an exemplar or slow trace to the failing span. Open logs by traceId . Confirm resource saturation: pool, GC, lag. Mitigate first (roll back, scale, shed load), then fix. SPRING Spring Boot setup // build.gradle dependencies spring-boot-starter-actuator micrometer-registry-prometheus micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel # application.yml management: endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,prometheus endpoint.health.probes.enabled: true tracing.sampling.probability: 0.1 metrics.distribution: percentiles-histogram: http.server.requests: true Keep sampling low in production; use tail sampling if you need all errors. COLLECTOR OpenTelemetry Collector shape receivers: otlp: {protocols: {grpc: {}, http: {}}} processors: memory_limiter: {check_interval: 1s, limit_percentage: 80} batch: {} exporters: # one per backend service: pipelines: traces: receivers: [otlp] processors: [memory_limiter, batch] exporters: [ ] metrics: {...} # → Prometheus logs: {...} # → Loki Exporter names depend on your backends; check the docs for your versions. QUERY PromQL and LogQL # request rate sum(rate( http_server_requests_seconds_count [5m])) # error ratio sum(rate( http_server_requests_seconds_count {status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate( http_server_requests_seconds_count [5m])) # p99 latency histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate( http_server_requests_seconds_bucket [5m]))) # LogQL {app="orders"} |= "ERROR" | json | traceId="4bf92f35..." W AT C H JVM and platform signals JVM jvm_memory_used_bytes, jvm_gc_pause_seconds, thread states DB pool hikaricp_connections_active, _pending, _timeout_total Kafka Consumer lag, rebalances, DLQ depth Pods Restarts, OOMKilled, CPU throttling DASHBOARDS Design a dashboard people use Top row: SLO and RED for the service. Second row: dependencies (DB, cache, downstream calls). Third row: resources (JVM, pool, CPU, memory). Annotate deploys and flag changes. Link panels to traces and logs. One purpose per dashboard; about a dozen panels at most. C O S T Anti-patterns and cost control Dashboards with 40 panels nobody reads: keep one RED page per service. Alerting on every error log line. High-cardinality labels: the fastest way to break Prometheus and the bill. Logging full request bodies: cost and privacy risk. Keeping everything at full resolution: set retention tiers, drop DEBUG, sample traces, downsample old metrics. No ownership: every dashboard and alert has a team. Monitoring tells you something is broken; observability lets you ask why. Alert on SLO burn, correlate by traceId, and keep cardinality and cost under control.

11 11 Production Incident Playbook What to do in the first ten minutes, how to triage by symptom, the commands for the JVM, host and database, and how to learn from it. INSIDE First ten minutes and the mitigation toolbox Symptom-to-cause triage table JVM, Linux and database commands Failure patterns and the postmortem outline THE ORDER Stabilise, communicate, investigate, learn THE ORDER A fast, boring rollback beats a clever diagnosis while users are down. First ten minutes FIRST 10 MINUTES Order of operations Acknowledge and assign roles: incident commander, ops lead, communications. Set severity using your organisation's definitions. Confirm impact: who, what, since when. Check the latest deploy and config changes. Mitigate before you find the root cause. Post the first status update. Start a timeline. Capture evidence before restarting anything. FIRST 10 MINUTES Mitigation toolbox Roll back Fastest fix when a recent deploy correlates Flag off Disable the new feature or path Scale out Buys time when saturated; may move the bottleneck Shed load Rate limit, drop non-critical traffic Fail over To replica, standby or another zone Circuit break Cut a failing dependency; serve degraded Restart Last resort. Take thread and heap dumps first COMMUNICATE Status update template Impact : what users see, and how many. Status : investigating, mitigating or monitoring. What we know : facts only. Next update : a specific time. Update on a fixed cadence, even with no news. Separate facts from hypotheses. One person owns external communication. Triage TRIAGE Symptom → likely cause → first check Latency up, CPU Waiting on I/O, locks or pool. Thread dump, low pool metrics Latency up, CPU Hot loop, GC, serialisation. Profile or high sample threads Errors after deploy Bad release or config. Diff, roll back 5xx from one dependency Downstream slow or down. Check timeouts and breakers Pool exhausted Slow queries, leaks, long transactions. Pool and DB metrics Consumer lag Slow handler, rebalance loop, poison message Memory climbing, OOM Leak or sizing. Heap histogram, heap dump Disk full Logs, temp, retention. df -h , du by directory Periodic spikes GC, cron, cache expiry. Correlate on a timeline Intermittent timeouts DNS, connection reuse, packet loss, noisy neighbour SIGNALS What to look at first Golden signals Latency, traffic, errors, saturation RED (services) Rate, errors, duration USE (resources) Utilisation, saturation, errors Percentiles Look at p95 and p99, not just the average Compare Against last week, same hour INVESTIGATE Questions that find the cause What changed? Deploy, config, flag, data, traffic, dependency. When exactly did it start? Match to the timeline. Who is affected? All users, one region, one tenant, one endpoint. Which signal moved first: latency, errors, saturation? Does it reproduce in staging or on one host? What does the dependency's own dashboard show? Commands J A V A JVM triage # hottest threads top -H -p printf '%x\n' # = nid in dump jcmd Thread.print > t.txt # memory and GC jstat -gcutil 1000 jcmd GC.heap_info jmap -histo:live | head -30 jcmd GC.heap_dump /tmp/h.hprof # profiling jcmd JFR.start duration=60s \ filename=/tmp/r.jfr Take two or three thread dumps a few seconds apart; one proves little. Enable HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError in production JVMs. H O S T Linux triage top # CPU, load vmstat 1 # run queue iostat -x 1 # disk free -m # memory df -h; df -i # space ss -s # sockets dmesg -T | tail # OOM kill journalctl -u svc -n 200 Use the USE method: utilisation, saturation and errors for each resource. DATABASE Database triage MySQL: SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST , SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS , slow query log. PostgreSQL: pg_stat_activity , pg_locks , pg_stat_statements . Look for long transactions, lock waits and a single query dominating load. Check connection count against the pool and the server limit. Check replication lag before reading from replicas. Do not kill sessions without knowing what they are. TOOLS Little's Law and saturation In flight = rate × latency. A rise in latency raises concurrency and can exhaust pools. Saturated resources grow queues; queues grow latency non-linearly. Retries multiply load. A retry storm can keep a recovering system down. Find the first saturated resource, fix it, then measure again. The bottleneck moves after each fix. Patterns and learning PATTERNS Failure patterns to recognise Retry storm Clients retry a struggling service. Add backoff, jitter and retry budgets Thundering herd Many callers wake at once. Stagger, jitter, queue Cache stampede Hot key expires, all miss. Lock, early refresh, stale-while-revalidate Cascading failure One slow dependency exhausts callers' threads. Timeouts, bulkheads, breakers Noisy neighbour Shared resource contention. Isolate or limit Slow leak Memory or connections grow until failure. Trend dashboards PITFALLS Mistakes that extend outages Changing several things at once, so you cannot tell what worked. Restarting before capturing evidence. Silence: no updates for long stretches. Chasing root cause while users are still impacted. Blaming people instead of finding system gaps. Declaring resolved without monitoring recovery. AFTER Blameless postmortem outline Summary, impact and duration. Timeline of detection, decisions and actions. Root cause and contributing factors (ask why repeatedly). What went well, what went badly, where we got lucky. Action items with owners and dates, prioritised. Detection gap: how could we have known sooner? PREVENT Operational readiness SLOs and alerts on symptoms, not only causes Runbooks for the top failure modes Dashboards with the four golden signals Timeouts, retries with jitter, circuit breakers Rollback tested and fast Feature flags for risky changes On-call rotation and escalation paths Game days or failure drills HANDOFF On-call handoff checklist Open incidents and current state Recent deploys and risky changes Known flaky alerts Pending follow-ups with owners Where the runbooks live Who to escalate to THE RULE Stabilise first, communicate early, investigate second, learn afterwards.

12 12 Git Production Incident Playbook What to run when a bad commit is live, history is lost, someone force-pushed, or a secret is in the repo. Stop the damage first, find the cause second, clean up last. INSIDE 26 scenarios, ordered by urgency Revert, bisect, reflog and rescue Force-push, wrong-branch and secret leaks Merge, rebase and conflict recipes BEFORE YOU RUN ANYTHING STOP THE BLEEDING Check first Roll back by artifact Run git status and git log --oneline -5 . Fastest safe mitigation. Confirm the branch and whether the commits are pushed. Replace placeholders such as <sha> , then read each command before pressing enter. Commands assume Git 2.23 or newer for switch and restore . git tag -a v1.4.2 -m "release" # redeploy previous tag v1.4.1 Tag every release. Prefer redeploying a known-good build over editing history. STOP THE BLEEDING FIVE RULES Hotfix flow Hold these in your head Fix prod without shipping unreleased work. Mitigate first. Revert or roll back, then investigate. Copy before surgery. git branch backup before any rewrite. Never rewrite shared history. main is append-only. git switch -c hotfix/x v1.4.1 # fix, test, tag, deploy git switch main git cherry-pick -x Port the fix to main, or it comes back in the next release. Reflog is the safety net. Local, and it expires. Rotate, then rewrite. A leaked secret is compromised the moment it is pushed. Find the cause Stop the bleeding FIND THE CAUSE Which commit broke it? Good tag exists, bad build doesn't. STOP THE BLEEDING Bad commit is live Prod is broken; the culprit is one pushed commit. git revert git push origin main # redeploy; investigate afterwards git bisect start git bisect bad git bisect good v1.4.1 git bisect run ./test.sh git bisect reset Needs a deterministic test. Skip untestable commits with git bisect skip. Revert, don't reset. History stays intact and CI/CD can redeploy. FIND THE CAUSE STOP THE BLEEDING Bad merge is live Who changed this line, when did this string appear? Trace a change. A merged PR broke prod. git log -S"text" --oneline git log -G"regex" -p -- path git log --follow -p -- path git blame -L 40,60 path git revert -m 1 -m 1 keeps the mainline parent. To re-merge the branch later, revert the revert first, or Git skips those changes. -S finds changes in occurrence count; -G matches diff lines by regex. STOP THE BLEEDING Revert a range Several commits must go. FIND THE CAUSE What shipped between releases? Scope the blast radius. git revert --no-commit old..new git commit -m "Revert X" git diff --stat v1.4.1 v1.4.2 git log --merges v1.4.1..v1.4.2 git log --oneline v1.4.1..v1.4.2 old is excluded, new is included. Review the diff before committing. Two dots on log = commits in the second not in the first. Undo local mistakes UNDO LOCAL Restore a file UNDO LOCAL Bring one file back from a commit. I lost commits (reset, bad rebase) git restore --source= -- path # discard local edits git restore path git reflog git switch -c rescue # or reset to a reflog entry git reset --hard HEAD@{n} Branch looks wrong; work seems gone. Doesn't touch history. Safe for single-file rollbacks. Reflog is local and expires (by default 90 days reachable, 30 unreachable). Act soon. UNDO LOCAL Abort a stuck operation Merge, rebase or cherry-pick went wrong. UNDO LOCAL Undo last commit, keep changes Unpushed commit was wrong. git merge --abort git rebase --abort git cherry-pick --abort # keep changes staged git reset --soft HEAD~1 # keep changes unstaged git reset HEAD~1 # discard changes git reset --hard HEAD~1 Aborting returns you to the pre-operation state. Shared-branch accidents SHARED BRANCH Only on unpushed commits. --hard destroys uncommitted work. Force-push overwrote teammates' work Remote branch lost commits. UNDO LOCAL # find the old tip git reflog show origin/main git push --force-with-lease \ origin :main git reflog git branch restored Deleted branch git branch -D by accident. The old tip may live in a teammate's clone or CI checkout. Pause pushes until it's restored. Find the tip in the reflog; the commits exist until garbage collected. SHARED BRANCH UNDO LOCAL Committed to main by mistake (unpushed) Detached HEAD with new commits Meant to use a feature branch. git switch feature You committed on a checkout of a tag or sha. git branch feature git reset --hard origin/main git switch -c rescue Do it before switching away, or find the sha in git reflog. If already pushed, use revert and open a PR instead. UNDO LOCAL SHARED BRANCH Dropped stash Committed to the wrong branch Stash is gone. Right commit, wrong place. git switch correct git cherry-pick git fsck --unreachable | grep commit git stash apply git switch wrong git reset --hard origin/wrong Works only until garbage collection. Check the commit message first. Confirm the cherry-pick landed before resetting the wrong branch. SHARED BRANCH BIG FILES Fix the last commit (unpushed) Stop tracking, keep locally Typo, missing file. File should be ignored. git add file git commit --amend git rm --cached path echo path >> .gitignore Amending rewrites the commit. Never on pushed shared branches. Doesn't remove it from history; see the secret playbook if sensitive. Secrets and big files Merge and rebase SECRETS MERGE & REBASE Secret was committed Conflicts keep recurring Key, token or password is in history. Same conflict on every rebase. # 1. revoke and rotate first git filter-repo \ --replace-text rules.txt git push --force --all git config rerere.enabled true rerere records and replays your resolutions. Rotation is the fix. Rewriting history is cleanup; forks and caches may keep the data. MERGE & REBASE “ours” and “theirs” look swapped Resolving during a rebase. SECRETS Remove a file from all history # rebase: upstream version git checkout --ours path # rebase: your commit git checkout --theirs path git filter-repo \ --path secrets.env --invert-paths Credentials file or dump committed. In a rebase, ours is the branch you're rebasing onto; in a merge it's your current branch. git filter-repo is a separate install. Everyone re-clones afterwards. MERGE & REBASE BIG FILES Huge file committed Rebase or merge? Integrating long-lived work. Repo bloated, pushes rejected. git merge --no-ff feature # linear, local only git rebase main # keep branch shape git filter-repo \ --strip-blobs-bigger-than 10M # going forward git lfs track "*.bin" Rebase only your private branches. Never rebase shared history. Large binaries belong in LFS or artifact storage. THE RULE Revert before you reset, copy before you rewrite, and rotate a leaked secret before you clean the history.
